roles: disciple of the Maggid of Mezeritch
summary: Meshulam Zusha of Anipoli (c. 1718-1800), a brother of Elimelech of Lizhensk and, with him, a disciple of Dov Ber, the Maggid of Mezeritch, was one of the early Hasidic masters of the Maggid's circle who helped spread the movement in the later eighteenth century. In the tradition's account and in the hagiographic anthologies he is remembered above all as a figure of simple, joyful, and self-effacing piety, the paradigm of the humble tzaddik, and as the subject of many devotional tales, among them the saying that in the world to come he would be asked not why he had not been Moses but why he had not been Zusha. Because he committed little to writing, what is transmitted of him comes largely through Hasidic hagiography and the traditions of his brother's circle.
description:
Meshulam Zusha of Anipoli (Hanipol, in Volhynia), who lived from about 1718 to 1800, was a brother of Elimelech of Lizhensk and, together with him, a disciple of Dov Ber, the Maggid of Mezeritch, the principal successor of the Baal Shem Tov. In the movement's account the two brothers were among the inner circle of the Maggid's students, and after their teacher's death (1772) they were among those who carried Hasidism outward through Volhynia, Galicia, and southern Poland in the decades of its rapid growth and of the organized Mitnagdic opposition to it. Where Elimelech became known as a systematic exponent of the doctrine of the tzaddik in his book No'am Elimelech, Zusha is remembered in the tradition less for a written corpus than for the manner of his piety and for the tales told of him; he committed little to writing, and his teachings survive chiefly as they were gathered by others.

The image of Zusha transmitted in Hasidic hagiography, and given fullest literary form in Martin Buber's retelling of the Hasidic tales, is that of a master of joyful, wholehearted, and radically humble service, often cast as the holy simpleton whose closeness to God expressed itself in fervent prayer, acceptance of suffering, and self-abnegation rather than in learning or leadership display. This picture is presented here as the tradition's attributed and hagiographic portrait, not as documentary biography: the tales exalt his humility and devotion for the edification of the reader, in the manner of the Hasidic praise-tale genre. The best known of these is the saying attributed to him that in the world to come he did not fear being asked 'Why were you not Moses?' but rather 'Why were you not Zusha?', a formulation preserved in Buber's collection and widely repeated as an epigram of self-realization and humility; it is recorded here as an attributed teaching-tale, not as a saying with independent documentary attestation.

In the modern scholarship Zusha appears mainly as one of the disciples of the Maggid's circle and as a foil to his brother Elimelech in accounts of the emergence of Hasidic leadership: studies of the doctrine and social institution of the tzaddik (Arthur Green; the essays gathered in Hasidism Reappraised) treat the Maggid's students as the generation in which the model of the rebbe as charismatic holy leader took shape, with Elimelech and Zusha offering contrasting types, the one an exponent of the tzaddik as active channel of divine flow, the other a paradigm of the humble and self-effacing saint. This entry presents Zusha on the tradition's own terms as the brother of Elimelech, a disciple of the Maggid, and a revered early master, while marking clearly that the material about him is largely hagiographic and that the scholarly treatment of him is thin and set within the wider study of the Maggid's circle and of Hasidic leadership.
editorial_notes: This entry presents Zusha of Anipoli on Judaism's own terms as the brother of Elimelech of Lizhensk, a disciple of the Maggid of Mezeritch, and a revered early Hasidic master, and is HONEST that the material about him is largely HAGIOGRAPHIC. His portrait as the humble, joyful, self-effacing tzaddik and the famous 'Why were you not Zusha?' saying are presented AS attributed Hasidic praise-tale and teaching-legend (given fullest form in Buber's literary retelling), DESCRIBED and not adjudicated, and NOT treated as documentary fact (neutrality #1, #4, #5), mirroring how the baal-shem-tov and shivchei-ha-besht entries handle hagiography. The Hasidic-Mitnagdic conflict is given as historical context, not adjudicated. Sources: (a) Martin Buber, Tales of the Hasidim: The Early Masters, cited explicitly as a curated literary anthology of Hasidic legend (attributed hagiography), not as history; (b) Arthur Green, 'The Zaddiq as Axis Mundi in Later Judaism' (JAAR 1977), for the academic treatment of the doctrine and figure of the tzaddik within which Zusha is placed; (c) the essays in Ada Rapoport-Albert, ed., Hasidism Reappraised (Littman Library, 1996), for contemporary scholarship on early Hasidic leadership and the Maggid's circle. No encyclopedias (no Encyclopaedia Judaica, no YIVO Encyclopedia, no Chabad.org, no My Jewish Learning), no Wikipedia, no tertiary sources. CONFIDENCE / HONESTY: this entry rests LARGELY on hagiography (Buber) and on general scholarship on the Maggid's circle rather than on a monograph devoted to Zusha or on an open primary read verbatim; there is no critical monograph on Zusha comparable to Rosman or Etkes on the Besht. It is therefore left at status DRAFT, and all three sources are rated medium, verified to exist and be on-topic (Schocken record and Internet Archive for Buber; Oxford Academic/JSTOR for the Green article; Littman Library / Liverpool University Press for Hasidism Reappraised), not read line-by-line. No claim about Zusha is asserted as established biographical fact beyond his kinship to Elimelech, his discipleship under the Maggid, and his approximate dates. lifespan.note: c. 1718-1800 CE. A brother of Elimelech of Lizhensk (b. 1717); the sources differ on which of the two was the elder. With him a disciple of Dov Ber, the Maggid of Mezeritch (d. 1772). He settled at Anipoli (Hanipol) in Volhynia, where he died in 1800. Dates are approximate; his biography is transmitted largely through Hasidic hagiography rather than documentary sources.

relations.note: Zusha was a brother of Elimelech of Lizhensk; the two are paired in the tradition's account as disciples of the Maggid who together carried Hasidism into Galicia and southern Poland, and are often contrasted as the humble saint (Zusha) and the systematic exponent of the doctrine of the tzaddik (Elimelech).
Zusha was a disciple of Dov Ber, the Maggid of Mezeritch, in whose circle of students he and his brother Elimelech studied and from which they went out to spread Hasidism.

Zusha was a Hasidic master of the third generation, a disciple of the Maggid's circle, and one of those who helped spread the movement in the later eighteenth century. The hasidism entry (a school) exists.

In the scholarship on the doctrine and institution of the tzaddik, Zusha is treated as a paradigm of the humble, self-effacing saint, contrasted with his brother Elimelech's account of the tzaddik as active channel of divine flow; given as the tradition's and the scholarship's attributed characterization. The tzaddik concept exists.
